038e5b1dfbb4.author: Ben Kelly
038e5b1dfbb4.html:
This week you may have seen an interview going viral where an LA City Councilmember says that to increase affordable housing in her district, she forced an affordable housing project to shrink and add more parking. This contradiction, where to support affordable housing she killed affordable housing, was lost on Councilmember Imelda Padilla. She talked about this as if it was a brave action she took to help the community.

This bizarre attitude is unfortunately common in politics, where if an official talks long enough, they can convince themselves that the best way to get people housing is to stop it from ever being built. I am going to highlight two NIMBY LA elected officials with different excuses for why they block housing, but these attitudes can be found in elected officials across the country.

Imelda Padilla and Local Control

Councilmember Padilla’s website lists the “unsheltered population” as her first priority, promising to implement an immediate solution to the housing crisis. Despite making such a bold claim, her actions speak differently.

Earlier this year, California State Senator Scott Weiner introduced SB 79, which would allow for more multi-family housing near rail stations and bus rapid transit (BRT) statewide. Almost 200,000 people in California do not have a home and housing prices are skyrocketing, so one would think that local officials would rejoice at the opportunity to build more housing. Yet Councilmember Padilla and many other California elected officials are officially opposing the bill, stating that it will take away local control.

To an extent, the Councilmember is right. An individual official will have less power to interfere in housing development if SB 79 passes. No politician likes losing power, but when they are using that power to block housing, it must be done. With SB 79, Councilmember Padilla would not have been able to cut that affordable housing development in favor of parking.

The most revealing aspect is how Padilla defended her actions against affordable housing. She said it with pride as an example of her work for the community. Politicians love to talk, and if you give them enough time they will be able to defend anything. If you were just casually listening to her, you would think that she was an advocate for housing. But you need to cut through the noise and listen for the substance of what she is saying. She is saying that she forced the affordable housing development to cut down from seven to three stories and to remove housing and put in more parking instead. It does not matter how many times she said “listen to the community” or “engage all stakeholders”, what matters is that she blocked housing.

Any time an elected official gives a defense of NIMBYism, listen closely, tuning out the standard politician platitudes. You will hear the same points that Councilmember Padilla stated, where “the community” does not want affordable housing and therefore it is her obligation to block said housing.

Karen Bass and “Unintended Consequences”

Karen Bass was elected as LA’s Mayor in 2022 while promising to take serious action on the housing crisis, but has proved to be a major disappointment. She has repeatedly taken action to block housing development in her city while making excuse after excuse for why housing should be blocked. Like Councilmember Padilla, Mayor Bass is rhetorically in favor of housing but in practice is a NIMBY.

In 2023 she signed an order to expedite affordable housing development in the city. This is a great idea, as municipalities’ permitting times and endless studies are major contributors to the housing crisis. However, as soon as Mayor Bass received pushback, she retreated and changed the order so that affordable housing near single family zoning was ineligible to be fast tracked. When that was not enough, she even further restricted it to block fast-tracking in historic districts or on properties with rent controlled apartments. This blocking in historic districts was at the request of homeowners in a wealthy LA neighborhood named Windsor Village. Developers had proposed building a 70 unit affordable housing development on a vacant lot in Windsor Village, so she made this change to slow that project down.

She later argued that blocking this affordable housing was a way to prevent gentrification. I do even know where to begin with that statement as it is completely detached from reality. In case anyone is unaware, affordable housing does not cause gentrification. Either Mayor Bass is so unaware of housing that she thinks this is true, or she is lying.

She received a lot of criticism for this statement, and she seems to have changed her words but still has the same message. Now she warns of “unintended consequences” in response to housing development, and then does not articulate what those consequences would be.

Mayor Bass has officially come out against SB 79 because of its “unintended consequences” and wants LA exempted from it. What a surprise that yet again, she speaks in favor of housing generally but opposes any attempt to actually build it.

This nebulous fear of “unintended consequences” is a common talking point from NIMBYs. It has a grain of truth, in that there may be unintended consequences from anyone taking action on anything. There may be unintended consequences if I go to the store, but I still have to get groceries.

I want to remind Councilmember Padilla and Mayor Bass of the intended consequences of their actions. Their actions blocked affordable housing. I do not care what long statement they would put out talking about their extensive community engagement and how they engaged all stakeholders. They had a binary choice between supporting or blocking housing, and they chose to block.

1da8590895da.author: Ben Kelly
1da8590895da.html:
The Case for Parking Tickets

Nobody likes walking back to their car and seeing that little white sheet on the windshield meaning they will have to pay $65 for a parking ticket. I have been in that situation multiple times, and I can promise you I was never happy about it. But I also know that it is a necessary part of life in an organized society, and that if we did not have parking tickets, life in the city would be worse.

Disliking tickets but saying they make life better may sound contradictory, but I think it is the logical conclusion. I believe consistent enforcement of parking rules in a city is necessary for three reasons: revenue, equity, and quality of life.

Cities raise a significant amount of money through parking tickets and fines, with my home city of Cincinnati collecting $4.1 million in fines in 2025 (or roughly $13 per resident). Cincinnati has a total budget of almost $600 million, so while it is not one of the city’s primary funding mechanisms, it does bring in real money.

Of course, Cincinnati is not alone in collecting these fines. New York City brings in over $500 million each year in parking tickets ($63 per resident), and Milwaukee collected $17 million ($30 per resident) in 2025.

If we stopped collecting tickets, the government would have to either raise taxes or cut spending to make up for that. Perhaps in Cincinnati that would be $4 million less of roads repaved in a year, or less frequent trash pickup, or maybe they would have to raise fees for summer camps or other city programs. To me, forgiving illegal parking is not worth the financial tradeoff.

Source: TikTok/RossLannon

When cars are parked illegally, it can hurt people. While I am walking around downtown, if there is a car on the sidewalk I can simply walk around it. But what if I were a blind person or a wheelchair user? Does the driver’s desire to park wherever they want trump the disabled person’s right to move freely through the city sidewalks?

Cars are often ticketed for parking in bus stops. A delay in the bus schedule might not be the end of the world, but it would disrupt the lives of many people, particularly lower income or working class individuals who use the bus for transportation. Does the driver’s desire to find an easy parking spot trump their right to use reliable public transportation?

When it comes to fires, every second counts. The reason that cars are ticketed for parking in front of hydrants is that they are directly blocking a firefighter from doing their job. This is a real problem, such as in January when the New York Fire Department were delayed from responding to a five-alarm fire because the three closest fire hydrants all had cars parked in front of them¹. Does the driver’s desire to spend less time looking for parking trump people’s right to safety?

When I go to the grocery store, I always return my shopping cart to the corral. I do this even though it might be a bit out of my way or it is raining or I am in a hurry, and even though I know that the damage of leaving my cart out would be minimal. But at the same time, if everyone left the cart out, the grocery store would be pure chaos. It works the same with parking.

If one person parks illegally, it is a minor inconvenience to the neighborhood. If twenty people park illegally, it could pose a serious disruption. By telling people that parking rules do not matter, we are saying those disruptions do not matter. Increasing enforcement of parking rules does improve compliance and increases the quality of life for citizens. In New York City, after the city began consistently enforcing rules against parking in bus lanes, residents complied and bus speeds increased by 30%².

As I stated earlier, nobody ever likes getting these tickets, and it is true that a $60-or-so fine can be a major hassle, especially to someone who is already living paycheck-to-paycheck. Some cities have implemented tiered fine structures, where lower income residents pay a smaller fine, such as in DC where SNAP recipients can apply for a 50% reduction in ticket fines for speeding³. I think that is a brilliant system and I would encourage cities to look into it and even expand it to cover parking tickets, but there must still be a fine issued to discourage illegal parking. If we are afraid of enforcing the law because people find it inconvenient, then we might as well stop enforcing the speed limit or DUI laws because it might hurt a driver’s wallet, nevermind the real harm this would cause to society.

I understand the desire to waive or limit ticket fees because of worries over cost of living and the economy, but before cities consider doing so, they must think about the cost. As I have shown in this piece, the cost is not just lost revenue for the government, but lost time for commuters, lost mobility for the disabled, and lost safety for residents.

¹https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/01/06/illegally-parked-cars-delayed-fdny-response-to-five-alarm-fire

²https://cal.streetsblog.org/2023/03/14/blocking-bus-lanes-doesnt-just-delay-transit-riders

³https://fine-reduction-faqs.dc.gov/

663997b0246f.author: Ben Kelly
663997b0246f.html:
City leaders often talk of the different factors hurting housing affordability right now: tariffs, cost of labor, and supply chain issues are three of the most cited in my experience. While those three are indeed impacting the cost of housing, they are for the most part out of City Hall’s control. One under-cited cause of the housing crisis is the municipal permit process, sometimes making City Hall its own worst enemy for affordability. As cities struggle to issue timely permits, housing and development in them stagnates.

A recent paper by Leonardo D’Amico, Evan Soltas, and Audrey Wang titled “Where Is Housing Slow to Build, And Is It Getting Slower?¹” examined the permitting process in 60 US cities to find the typical timeline before a project is completed. Their results paint a frustrating picture of cities being slow to respond to the need for more housing.

The worst offenders were coastal cities like New York, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. In those cities, it takes an average of two and a half years for a single family home to be completed, with multi-family units taking four years. While their mayors seek to increase the supply of housing, an apartment that starts development today will take an entire mayoral term before it is complete. Compared to those cities, Sunbelt cities such as Raleigh, Orlando, and Phoenix complete a single family home in a year and a multi-family in two.

I am not aware of any benefits that the residents of Los Angeles and San Francisco receive from these cities’ long permitting processes. The housing built in Raleigh is just as safe as the units built in Los Angeles so it does not seem like the Sunbelt cities are hastily rushing permits through with insufficient oversight.

Disappointingly, even as technology has improved, permitting times have more than doubled over the last 25 years. D’Amico, Soltas, and Wang found that the probability of a multi-family project being approved within six months fell from 71% to 44%. Their study also estimates that a one year increase in permitting duration on average leads to a 39% increase in median rent for the unit. The longer these projects are in limbo, the higher the cost.

This does not have to be the case. Compared to 2000, the technology available to planning departments is miles ahead. Instead of manually looking through a physical zoning code, planners can search through it digitally while looking at properties on Google Maps and GIS systems which should theoretically streamline the process, not slow it down.

I want to be clear that the blame does not rest on the city planners themselves here. They are public servants who are pursuing a complex field where they have to deal with many competing interests. Unfortunately, over the last 25 years, politicians have bogged down municipal zoning codes. They add more mandatory community meetings, stricter zoning rules, more stages of review, and other instances of red tape.

And the politicians themselves most likely did not implement those requirements with the intent of blocking housing, but that is the effect. Each of the regulations was made with good intentions, but good intentions do not automatically produce affordability. As more and more red tape is added, fewer homes get built and housing gets more expensive.

As a Democrat, I am frustrated with all these blue cities failing to meet the moment on housing. States like California and New York are losing population to Florida and Texas, and a major reason is that those are states that are building housing and getting prices down.

If Democrats want to get in power to implement their preferred policies, we need to show that Democrats know how to govern so people stop moving away from these blue coastal states to the red Sunbelt states. In the 2030 congressional reapportionment, Texas and Florida are estimated to gain 3 or 4 seats each while California is projected to lose up to four. That means more congressional representation for those states and more power in the electoral college. To grow the population in these blue states, we need to get serious about reform.

It feels odd to be a Democrat advocating for cutting regulations and red tape. Often when I call for speeding up government or reducing regulations, my progressive friends will joke that I am secretly a Republican, but the reality is that I believe in the power and promise of government, and I recognize that we need to have an effective City Hall to show that Democrats can govern. Right now cities are burying themselves in red tape and are losing residents as a result.

The good news is that plenty of municipalities have noticed these problems as well and are looking for solutions. The most basic is simplifying the zoning code. Legislators have added more and more requirements to these codes while rarely removing any regulations. This results in these unwieldy zoning codes that confuse even experienced city planners. Burbank, California, streamlined its zoning code and removed certain requirements in 2022, with city officials estimating that the changes could cut their permitting time in half².

Some cities have created accountability systems to show their commitment to speeding up the process. Denver implemented a 180-day “shot clock” for permitting, guaranteeing a city response to permit requests within that timeframe. If the city fails to do so, the permit applicant is entitled to up to $10k in fee refunds. San Diego chose a more focused approach called Affordable Housing Permit Now (AHPN): a 30-day “shot clock” for income-restricted affordable housing. While Denver’s shot clock was just implemented in 2025 and has little public data, San Diego’s model has been a proven success. According to the city, AHPN has resulted in 2,848 completed affordable homes, 1,589 homes under construction and 2,809 homes currently in the review process and has also supported 387 emergency shelter beds³.

Of course, cities must have the capacity to get these permits done correctly. Simplifying the code helps, but an even faster route chosen by some cities is to implement AI in permitting review.

Honolulu and Seattle are two cities that have done so and experienced positive results. Both cities contracted with CivCheck, a platform that examines applications and compares them with a city’s zoning code to check for completeness. Applicants upload their forms into CivCheck’s system, and they receive a near-instant reply telling them if the application is complete or not. After a completed review is uploaded, it goes to the human reviewers in the city department for final review. Honolulu has a long-term contract while Seattle ran a pilot and is now pursuing a longer-term test after the success of the initial term. The state of California arranged for a different AI permitting vendor called Archistar to help process applications for rebuilding after the 2025 wildfires.

While it is still a new technology, AI permitting has so far shown to be a success for both cities and applicants. It sped up the permitting process and helped housing get built faster. As more and more housing breaks ground through these faster permits, residents will start seeing cheaper housing and more vibrant cities.

I have heard from others in city government worried that this technology would result in city planners being laid off. That result strikes me as unlikely. I do not know a single city planner who says that they are underworked or they like doing simple completeness checks on applications. This technology instead allows the planner to focus more on the complex and technical elements of the applications while the basic yet time-consuming tasks are done by AI.

Even if one is against the use of AI in permitting review, hopefully all can agree that cities benefit from reduced permitting times. These backlogs make housing more expensive and prevent cities from growing, but the good news is that the solution is entirely within City Hall’s control. If leaders prioritize permitting, they can make real progress towards affordability.

¹https://evansoltas.com/papers/Durations_DSW2026.pdf

²https://www.facebook.com/fb-answers/burbank-construction-regulations/

³ https://www.insidesandiego.org/citys-affordable-housing-permit-now-program-earns-regional-recognition

⁴https://www.gov.ca.gov/2025/04/30/governor-newsom-announces-launch-of-new-ai-tool-to-supercharge-the-approval-of-building-permits-and-speed-recovery-from-los-angeles-fires/

⁵https://seattle.gov/documents/Departments/Performance/Publications/2026CivCheckEvaluationReport.pdf

6b27d761b18f.author: Ben Kelly
6b27d761b18f.html:
As Graham Platner’s nightmare of a campaign comes to an ugly end, it is important to look back and see how we got here. Some left him after the Nazi tattoo, some after the Reddit posts, some after the cheating, but others stuck by him until the rape accusation. I believe even if none of those details ever became public that Platner would still have underperformed in Maine. His candidacy rested on a flawed premise — that Maine wants a firebrand, anti-establishment progressive.

Supporters would argue that Maine showed exactly that desire with Platner’s win in the primary, but a primary is different from a general. To his credit, Platner was able to run a very effective campaign to win the Democratic primary. Unfortunately, that is only the start of the battle.

Plenty of candidates have won primaries only to see their message not translate to the general election. Look at Christine O’Donnell, who in 2010 beat the popular sitting Congressman Mike Castle for the nomination for Senate in Delaware with the support of the Tea Party. Castle led his Democratic opponent by double digits in every poll, but he narrowly lost to O’Donnell in the primary. She then went on to lose what was at one point a certain gain for the GOP.

Platner did not even face a particularly strong primary field. Governor Janet Mills entered the race late and ran a half-hearted campaign and most of the other potential candidates decided to run for Governor instead of Senate. In the general, he would face a formidable opponent in Susan Collins. Collins was outraising him and had more cash on hand at the time he dropped out and was ahead of him in the polls. Crucially, she is also outperforming Platner with white working class voters, which was supposedly Platner’s base. Susan Collins is a soft spoken Senator who styles herself as a moderate¹ focused on bipartisanship and she was able to win over the non-college educated voters better than Platner.

Platner and his team would argue that Maine does not want some moderate dealmaker, they want a fighter. However, look at who has been winning elections in Maine. Susan Collins has won every six years since 1996. Their Governor is Janet Mills, who Platner’s campaign would call an establishment corporatist. The other Senator from Maine is Angus King, an Independent who caucuses with the Democrats. Senator King has done a good job separating himself from the Democratic brand in Maine, but he has done so by appealing to the center, not the left, and was ranked in 2023 as the fifth most bipartisan Senator. Congressman Jared Golden represents Maine’s second district and is the chair of the Blue Dog Coalition, a group of moderate to conservative Democrats. Where is this supposed progressive movement in Maine? It has not shown itself anywhere outside of Democratic primaries.

This is also true for other purple-to-red states. In North Carolina, moderate former Governor Roy Cooper is leading his Republican opponent in almost every poll. Is Cooper some firebrand progressive who talks about fighting the oligarchy? No, he is a centrist who is focused on cost of living and healthcare. He gets along with the party establishment and does not spend his time ranting about Chuck Schumer or the billionaires, yet he will most likely win a Senate seat in a state that voted for Donald Trump just two years ago.

The argument that Platner needed to be a different kind of Democrat is also flawed because Kamala Harris won Maine. The Democratic establishment that Platner was decrying had just won the state two years ago. If Platner just appealed to Harris voters, he would have won the general with no issue.

All of this would have been true even without his scandals. But as the scandals kept coming out and became worse and worse, it showed that there was a major flaw in candidate recruitment. It is clear that he is someone who appeals to young, progressive, college educated voters. He is an white collar worker’s idea of what a blue collar man looks like. He wears jeans, has facial hair and tattoos, and swears a lot. This is the same line of thinking that got young progressives to support John Fetterman and ignore his obvious red flags². In reality, politicians of all types can find different ways to appeal to working class voters. Susan Collins, a 73 year old woman who has spent the last thirty years in DC, was outperforming the gruff veteran outsider among working class voters.

Platner’s campaign ran a perfunctory vetting process that missed many of his controversies and seemed to not care about major ones such as his Reddit posts. For context, his Reddit posts had many disturbing elements, perhaps the most horrifying one was from 2013 and blamed women for getting too drunk and being raped. At the time he posted that, Platner was a 29 year old man.

Yes, everyone has said stupid or terrible things in their life (though I would argue that Platner’s statements are more egregious than usual). But Platner did not stop there. Even after assuring people there were no more skeletons in his closet, we saw his Nazi tattoo. I do not think Graham Platner is a secret Nazi, but I do think the tattoo shows he is a man with terrible judgement who should not be trusted to make important decisions for our country. Then it came out that he was cheating on his wife at the start of the campaign, then the allegations of abuse from an ex girlfriend came out, and finally the accusation of rape from a different ex girlfriend was brought to light. It is shocking, but not at all surprising.

Even his video announcing his withdrawal showed him to be an unsavory person. He made no apologies and said that he was only leaving because the establishment was forcing him to do so. If the establishment has a policy of forcing rapists out, I support the establishment on that one.

Outsiders can make great candidates and politicians. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was a bartender just before going to Congress, and I think her experience has made her a talented communicator and she has shown an ability to adapt and grow in office. One of Barack Obama’s main appeals in his 2008 race was that he was not a creature of Washington and had only been in the Senate for four years. Nobody would argue that “the establishment” is popular or that candidates should tie themselves to it, but the opposite of the establishment is not some creep who posts about rape on Reddit. Platner was not the guy for this campaign and that was clear long ago.

The Main Democratic Party has a real opportunity to switch things around here. Prediction markets are hardly a scientific measure, but it is telling that on both Kalshi and Polymarket the chance of a Democratic victory in Maine increased after Platner withdrew.

I do not pretend to know who would be the right fit for Maine or what faction of the party should decide the new nominee. All I know is that it should be someone who appeals to Mainers of all political stripes, not just overly online firebrands.

¹Emphasis on the words “styles herself”. Collins’ record does not match her moderate claims.

²Full transparency: I am one of those young college educated progressives who supported Fetterman in 2022.

8d78c710b062.author: Ben Kelly
8d78c710b062.html:
Some of the worst ideas in government are the ones that sound good on paper. One (possibly apocryphal) example is during British rule of colonial Delhi, in an attempt to bring down the cobra population, the government offered a cash bounty for every dead cobra. This led to scores of people bringing in dead cobras for the bounty. Sounds like a good idea, problem solved, right?

Unfortunately, the bounty system led to people breeding cobras just to kill them for the bounty. When the British heard about this, they ended the bounty system and the cobra breeders released all of their cobras, creating an even larger population of cobras than before the bounty system. In their attempt to cull the cobras, the colonial government set up a system that created even more cobras.

While not as deadly, America has a somewhat similar counterintuitive system to solve a problem. The US has a massive shortage of affordable housing, so on paper it sounds like a good idea to require that a certain percentage of new housing be rented at an affordable price. Many cities throughout the country have implemented these Inclusionary Zoning (IZ) rules to force developers to include more affordable units. This is a worthy goal, but similar to the cobra bounties, in practice it is counterintuitive and can make the problem worse according to a new paper released last month from UC Irvine.

Before I worked in government, I looked at all the housing developments being approved by the local government and thought to myself “Why don’t they just require that a certain percentage of the housing has cheaper rent? That way developers would be forced to produce affordable housing.” I did not know I was just describing Inclusionary Zoning. Unfortunately, the quick and easy solution rarely pans out in practice.

In Noah Kouchekinia’s study “Inclusionary Zoning and Housing Supply: Evidence from California’s Palmer Fix¹”, the author examines the effects of IZ in California, which had a unique situation that made it a good test case for IZ. A 2009 court ruling, Palmer v. LA, effectively struck down IZ in California, labeling it as an illegal form of rent control, until 2017 when the state legislature updated the state code with a so-called “Palmer Fix” to allow IZ again. This 8 year period gives a clear before-and-after of IZ and its effects on housing production as IZ enforcement was suddenly cut off in 2009 before resuming in 2017.

I would recommend people read the full study to get a better understanding of its methodology, but in short it looked at the various forms of IZ in California cities and assigned it a rating based on the strictness of the policy and examined how much rent a landlord would have to forgo in the city. In many studies, researchers use a binary “Has IZ / Does Not Have IZ” designation, but the strictness of the IZ policy is critical. For example, a requirement that 20% of new units be affordable causes more foregone rent than a 10% requirement. The definition of “affordable” is also important, with some localities having it set at a lower income level than others.

This measure of stringency is important when people point to cities like Minneapolis as a positive example of IZ. Minneapolis has been able to produce a large number of units over the last few years while having an IZ policy, but Minneapolis’s policy is fairly minor. It only applies to developments with more than 20 units and requires only 8% of the development to be moderately affordable. In contrast, Santa Monica in 1998 enacted a requirement that 30% of all new housing, even in smaller developments, be rented at even more affordable levels than Minneapolis. Purely on paper, it sounds like Santa Monica should have cheaper housing, but in practice it is the opposite. For research purposes, it is essential to acknowledge the difference between Minneapolis and Santa Monica’s housing policies.

Kouchekinia’s study measured how much rent was being foregone due to these IZ policies. For example, if there were no IZ policies in place, then a landlord would rent every unit at market rate. With an IZ ordinance, they would have to rent a certain number of units at a lower rate. Under Santa Monica’s rules, if a new building has 50 units and market rent is $2,000/month each ($100,000/month total if fully market rate), the city requires 30% of units (15 units) to be affordable to low-income tenants, meaning rent capped at $1,200/month for those units instead of $2,000. That’s $12,000/month in forgone rent across the building ($800 x 15), against the $100,000/month market-rate baseline. The landlord will either have to eat the cost of that $12,000/month, or they will charge the other units approximately $350 more per month to make up for it. While that is good news for those 15 people who were lucky enough to get the IZ units, it means that all the other tenants are paying more to subsidize those units. That is also only if they can find tenants at that higher rate. If they are charging over 10% higher than market rate for the units, the landlord will have trouble filling those units.

One could make a moral argument that they are fine with the wealthier tenants subsidizing the rent for the lower income residents, but Kouchekinia’s study determined that IZ actually reduces the amount of housing that is built in a city. In his examination of 575 different California localities, the author determined that for every additional percentage point of rent foregone under an IZ rule, new housing permits are reduced by about 7.6%. Of the 575 California jurisdictions examined in the study, the average rent being foregone in areas with IZ was 4.2%, meaning that California’s typical IZ ordinance reduced the number of units being built by almost 32%.

Kouchekinia found that renters in IZ jurisdictions in California paid about $6.97 billion in additional rent due to the IZ policies which produced 8,990 low-income units during that window. On average, each affordable unit cost $775,000 in excess rent paid by the other renters. The author points out that this is far higher than the cost of subsidizing low-income housing through the Low Income Housing Tax Credit program (LIHTC), which has an average marginal cost in California of $441,000. In addition, while the cost of LIHTC is paid for by the government, the affordable unit subsidy from IZ is paid for by other renters. It should be noted that on average, renters already have lower income than homeowners, so it is not like the mega rich are the ones paying under IZ.

This study adds to the growing body of literature and data showing the dangers of IZ. While the policymakers may have had good intentions, like the creators of the cobra bounties, they have just made the problem worse.

¹The full paper can be read here: https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/sites.uci.edu/dist/b/5302/files/2026/06/IZ_Kouchekinia.pdf

d50b7df48bfd.author: Ben Kelly

Tooth decay hits the poor and vulnerable the hardest. Children from low income families are twice as likely to have cavities as their wealthier counterparts¹. This disparity also hurts the disabled and those in rural communities who will have a harder time finding care.

For those with insurance, a cavity may just mean an annoying visit to the dentist where they get a filling. But for those who cannot get treatment, that cavity will cause them chronic pain and eventually lead to much worse health outcomes and potentially even lead to death.

It is recommended that people go to the dentist every six months for a professional cleaning and a checkup. The vast majority of the time is spent on the teeth cleaning by a dental hygienist, only for the dentist to make a brief appearance at the end and briefly look around before concluding the visit for a typical cost upwards of $100.

As people look for ways to increase affordability and access to healthcare, I started looking into how oral healthcare could become cheaper for the average family. After looking at the existing systems and many studies, I believe there are structural barriers that the state of Ohio has implemented that are reducing access to dental care simply because of political connections and the influence of money in politics.

It is clear that getting more people to have regular cleanings will have a positive effect on public health, and there are certain unnecessary regulatory barriers right now increasing the cost of cleanings. One major piece of red tape in Ohio law is the requirement that dental hygienists primarily work in a dental practice with the dentist physically in the building. While this may not seem like a big deal, it has major consequences and prevents some vital work from being performed.

Even though the person doing most of the work during a teeth cleaning is a dental hygienist who makes an average of $94k per year, you are also paying for the dentist who makes at least double and often triple that. The dentist is doing little-to-no work during a cleaning, but the state of Ohio requires their presence which raises the cost considerably.

Not every state requires this. Colorado, Maine, New Mexico, and Washington allow hygienists to own and operate their own clinics offering teeth cleaning services, which gives people of those states a lower cost choice for teeth cleaning. It also allows hygienists more freedom to perform charitable services, which one dental hygienist named Anita Rodriguez did in Washington state for more than 20 years. Her independent practice, Elder Care Dental Hygiene, provided low cost dental cleaning in a mobile clinic for seniors and those with special needs. She also trained other hygienists to perform these good works, further increasing access to oral health care for those in need².

In addition to helping with charitable cases, it also gives hygienists more career opportunities and the ability to open up their own independent practice. This encourages more people to pursue a career as hygienists as it would increase the salary range and offer more flexibility.

A dental hygienist in Ohio only receives their license after completing more than 1,000 hours of supervised clinical practice, passing the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination, passing a separate regional clinical examination, and passing the Ohio Dental Practice Act jurisprudence exam. After all of that training though, the state of Ohio still says they need supervision and cannot operate independently as dental hygienists.

The only time that Ohio allows a hygienist to operate independently is through the Ohio Oral Health Access Supervision Program. This program allows hygienists to perform work independently in certain facilities³ to increase access to care. While this is a good step, the fine print shows that it still heavily restricts hygienists. To perform this charitable work, the hygienist needs a permit signed by a dentist that they work for and said dentist can authorize no more than three hygienists for this type of work. In addition, if they perform cleaning services for anyone, that individual must go to a dentist before a hygienist is allowed to clean for them again⁴. This shows that while the legislature does trust hygienists to work without supervision, it only does so when they will not receive significant compensation for their work.

If Anita Rodriguez from Washington tried to perform her mobile dental care work in Ohio, she would have had to work full time for a dentist, receive written permission before going to any facility to perform cleaning services, and would only be able to help a patient once and would not be able to return to them until that patient has seen a dentist. She also would not have been able to train other hygienists to carry on this work, further limiting access to dental care.

It is worth noting the gender aspect of this. Almost 95% of dental hygienists are women, but they make up less than 40% of dentists. This is a male dominated field of dentists saying that this woman dominated field of hygienists cannot be trusted to work without supervision.

When I see a situation like this, I look at what the potential barriers are to changing it — who is content with the current system and would dislike it changing, and what connections that group has.

Right now, this system greatly benefits dentists, specifically dentists who own their own practices. This means they do not have to compete with hygienists opening up their own cleaning clinics, which could deprive them of employees and increase their competition.

To be clear, I do not think the American Dental Association (ADA) is a nefarious organization secretly trying to give poor people unhealthy teeth. The truth is they are an organization whose primary goal is to support the interests of dentists, and if a dentist has to compete with independent hygienist clinics, they will have more competition for their services and may have a harder time hiring staff. It makes sense that the ADA fights against changes that may impact the financial bottom line.

Unfortunately, the system breaks down when one side is significantly more powerful than the other. The dental lobby is particularly powerful compared to the dental hygienist lobby. The ADA, which opposes independent teeth cleaning clinics, spent $1.84 million on lobbying in 2024 and contributed $2.5 million to campaigns⁵. Meanwhile, the American Dental Hygienist Association (ADHA), which states that hygienists should be able to operate independently, spends a negligible amount lobbying, and I am not able to find any PAC contributions on their behalf⁶. They are not funding politicians, which means they are not in the room with politicians when these rules are made.

State level lobbying is harder to track, but the Ohio Dental Association’s (ODA) website speaks of a daily presence at the Ohio Statehouse and says that 90% of their supported candidates won their races. Much of the work the ODA does is admirable, such as in 2023 when it helped convince legislators to almost double the funding for Ohio’s dental Medicaid program⁷. The ODA also has tremendous influence through the Ohio Dental Board, which is made up of nine dentists, three dental hygienists, and one unaffiliated member. The governor appoints members to the board after their names are put forward by the ODA and the Ohio Dental Hygienist Association (ODHA).

This gives the dentist lobby even more power, as the ODA is essentially choosing the people that will be making the rules regulating dentists and they control almost three quarters of the board.

The dental lobby has much more influence and money than the hygienist lobby, and the Ohio Dental Board is not going to recommend an action like this that increases competition for dentists. The only hope is that this can become a bipartisan issue where determined lawmakers of both parties work together to change the system.

This is not a right-or-left issue. It is not a liberal or a conservative move to give dental hygienists more freedom in their career options, it is just an evidence-based move to improve people’s health outcomes. The ADA and ODA should be consulted on all legislation related to dental care, but they should not be given complete control of the rules and regulations. Just because hygienists have fewer political connections does not mean they should need a dentists’ permission to clean teeth.
